text.p: Anglo-American engineering group LucasVarity Plc bought 10 million of its own shares Thursday, launching an 80 million British pound ($130 million) share buy-back programme and pushing forward its efforts to satisfy investors on both sides of the Atlantic.

"They have the authority to buy 42 million shares and they've made a big start buying about a quarter of that," said a spokesman at ABN AMRO Hoare Govett, which executed the deal for the company at 198 pence a share.

LucasVarity proposed a blend of buybacks and dividend growth -- from a reduced level -- on Tuesday when it released its first yearly results since the merger last year between Britain's Lucas and Varity Corp. of the United States.

The company said its yearly dividend of 2.25 pence (4 cents) per share, planned to rise to 4.5 percent for the year to January 31, 1998, would be supplemented with a buy-back of 3 percent of its outstanding shares, which could be repeated next year.
"This is a tax-efficient method of distributing the dividend for both the company and for shareholders with the share price at current levels," said SG Strauss Turnbull analyst Andy Crispin.

LucasVarity's share price has been under severe pressure in recent months amid market concerns about how it would reward investors, 60 percent of whom are in Britain and 40 percent in the United States.

Different approaches to rewarding shareholders had led to uncertainty about how the company would alter its dividend policy to keep both camps happy. Lucas investors were used to dividend growth and their payout last year was seven pence per share. Varity investors were accustomed to rewards from buy-backs.
LucasVarity shares shed 5 pence (8 cents) to 191-1/2 pence ($3.10) after Thursday's buy-back, reflecting market disappointment over the buy-back.
British companies usually buy back shares all at once, while a rolling programme is more common in the United States

"People hoped they'd make a quick turn out of this if LucasVarity came in and bought the shares in a lump, so it spiked up after they said they'd do the buy-back on Tuesday and now it's coming off because they're disappointed," said a dealer.
The shares rose to a session high of 208 pence ($3.30) on Tuesday immediately after the buy-back news.
